newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguans flock to register in tense elections.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguans flock to register in tense elections.

text.p: Using mules, canoes and helicopters, authorities made a last bid to deliver ballots to far-flung communities in Nicaragua on Saturday, as voters clammered to register a day before landmark presidential elections.

Long lines formed at voter registration offices ahead of a midday deadline for issuing credentials, but many were turned away empty handed. Supporters of each main party complained that the other was manipulating the voter lists.

In Nicaragua, scarred by a history of dictatorship and war, citizens have embraced democracy with a passion since the last elections in 1990, when the Marxist Sandinista government was toppled in a stunning upset at the ballot box.

"We've suffered so much war, authoritarianism and convulsion. We want peace and we want democracy," said Ernesto Francisco Vallejos, 37, a Nicaraguan who travelled from neighbouring Honduras to get his voting credential just before Saturday's deadline.

The passion to vote was bolstered by the heated nature of the contest, in which two old enemies, right-wing former Mayor Arnoldo Aleman of the Liberal Alliance and Sandinista ex-President Daniel Ortega were running almost neck and neck.
The latest CID-Gallup poll showed Aleman had a slight edge over Ortega, at 40.5 percent to 37.9 percent. If neither achieves 45 percent, the election goes to a second round.
Both strongmen have painted the other as a potential throwback to dictatorship, and the specter of the past has led supporters of each side to consider their vote crucial.

"The people now understand that totalitarianism doesn't work. We are tired of it, and we want to stop living on handouts from other countries. Democracy is the only way forward," said William Jimenez, 44, a pro-Sandinista salesman.
Unlike many nations in Latin America, authorities were not expecting a high level of abstention at the polls, in a country where politics rivals baseball as the national passion.
Flying in from Miami this week, supporters of Aleman, many who fled into exile during the 1979-1990 Sandinista years, chanted support for their candidate while airborne.
La Prensa newspaper on Saturday published photographs of Nicaraguans without passports illegally and perilously crossing the River Sapoa from neighbouring Costa Rica to vote.
Nicaragua's army, once the backbone of the Sandinista Front, has thrown its weight behind the electoral process and has pledged to respect the vote whichever way it goes.
On Saturday, army helicopters hopped through remote regions delivering ballot boxes to communities far from paved roads.

In an interview with Reuters on Friday, Commander-in-Chief Gen. Joaquin Cuadra Lacayo said 10,000 of the 14,500-strong force were involved in safeguarding the vote at 8,998 polling stations. Some 300 mules were used to carry ballot boxes to mountain and jungle communities, as well as canoes where they were the only access to river communities.
"For the first time, the bullets and bombs will be absent, and I'm sure that Nicaraguans, in spite of their fears, will vote in peace," he said.

Despite the unquestionable enthusiasm for democracy, organisational skills fell short. U.S. ex-President Jimmy Carter late on Friday estimated that four percent of the 2.4 million eligible voters had still not received credentials.

He also noted that with 23 candidates on the presidential ballot, the election was "the most complex" his 47-strong mission monitoring the elections had ever observed. Besides Aleman and Ortega, the 21 other candidates are only expected to muster a fraction of the vote.

Those unable to obtain credentials on Saturday complained that rival parties had sought to strike them off the voter lists, but election officials in Managua said there was no deliberate sabotage, just technical problems.
They said many potential voters were turned away because they had not registered in time.
